Recent Tragedies.
J. E. Oakes, aged 19, fatally stabbed R. T. Rainey, aged 15, at Danville, Va., on the night of the 31st ult.
At a political meeting at Balltown, Ky., on the 30th ult., Turner Wilson was fatally shot by Johnson, son of ex-Licut, Gov. Johnson.
Wm. Mackin shot and fatally wounded his brother Michael on the 1st instant, while the latter was trying to enter William's house, at Chicago. Michael had visited the house before that day and abused his brother's wife.
Near Oxford, N. C., on the 31st ult., a boy, 6 years of age, named Barton, threw his infant brother into a well where he was drowned.
An English missionary and his two servants have been murdered at Ismidt, Asia Minor, near Constantinople.
An armed mob of about 100 men from adjoining counties went into Moberly, Mo., on the 29th ult., and as Sheriff Mattock was taking J. C. Carlew into the court house to be tried for committing rape on the person of Mrs. Crump at the hotel in that city last March, opened fire on him. Carlew took to his heels but was finally cornered in a building where he was shot to death by the husband of his victim. Intense excitement prevailed while these violent proceedings were in progress and the officers of the law seemed paralyzed, as they made no effort to stop the butchery.
On the night of the 29th ult., a party of 15 masked men went to the house of Job Thompson, colored, about twenty miles from Atlanta, Ga., dragged him out, beat him and his wife fearfully, fatally shot his son, and killed his daughter. Great indignation is felt throughout the county. A citizens' meeting at Jonesboro denounced the killing, and offered $500 reward for the murderers. Thompson says he recognized as the leader of the gang John Gray, whom he recently prosecuted and had convicted of assault and battery.
A party of Creek Indians attacked two Cherokees near Gobson station, I. T., on the 28th, killing one and wounding another. The Creeks were incensed because two of their number were hanged by the Cherokees.
Mrs. Anna Lynch, of the Keystone house, Portland, Oregon, fatally stabbed Alex. Mattieson, who, she claims, made a dishonorable proposition and attempted an indecent assault.

Thomas Delana, proprietor of a livery stable at Chicago, was fatally stabbed about midnight of the 27th, by his wife, whom he was endeavoring to persuade to accompany him home.

Michael Maddox was arrested at Baltimore, Md., on the 27th, for killing John Schaba, a Bohemian. Maddox alleges that he found Schaba in his (Maddox's) wife's chamber.

Joseph Staats, a young man who was married only 19 days ago, was shot dead in his yard at Centralia, Ill., on the night of the 25th by some person unknown. Some think it a suicide while others believe it a murder.

John Diggs, the negro who outraged Mrs. James T. Chiffely on the night of the 24th, near Durnestown, Md., was taken from the jail at Rockwell, on the 27th, by an armed mob, and hung.

At a barn dance at Green Brier station, Robertson county, Tenn., on the 26th, Ben. Webster was mortally wounded with a stone, thrown by Tom Jones. Webster was one of the most substantial citizens of the county.

George Washington, a colored murderer, was recently hanged by a mob, in the backwoods of Tennessee.

A Mexican army officer being imprisoned at Monterey for drunkenness, his comrades stormed the jail, on the 26th, but were successfully resisted by the citizens and police. Three officers and fourteen men were killed or wounded in the melee.

Pat Kelly and Jack Brown, of Rochester, Pa., who had been on bad terms for years, met on the 25th inst. and "had it out." Kelly will die from pistol wounds received in the affray.

A son of Hon. D. N. Solomon, residing with his father on a farm about thirty miles from Council Bluffs, Ia., shot and killed one or two burglars who entered their premises, on the night of the 27th.

Dr. F. M. Williams, of Mechanicsburg, Miss., was assassinated while riding home on the night of the 24th inst. A negro arrested on suspicion confessed the crime, stating that he was paid to kill the doctor.

A party of roughs created a disturbance at a negro camp meeting near Cincinnati, Ohio, on the 25th instant, and a general row ensued. One of the roughs was perforated through the abdomen by a bullet, and several of the darkies were so badly hurt that they are not expected to survive. At Sag Harbor, N. Y., on the 26th instant, Miles Morris was shot dead by a scaman who accused Morris of being improperly intimate with the wife of the seaman. Dr. Alfred Lefevre was fatally shot in his office at Oakland, Cal., on 26th instant, by Edward Schroeder. Both parties were in good social position, the latter being a bank teller and the former a long established and popular dentist. Suspicion of criminal intimacy between Schroeder's wife and the murdered man led to the tragedy.
george-washington-denver-1880-07.A2:
CRIMINALITIES.
AWFUL PUNISHMENT OF A MISERABLE WRETCH,
J. C, Corlew, an ex-convict, under indictment at Moberly, Mo., for one of the basest crimes known to the law, committed in that city several months ago, upon the wife of a respectable citizen of Centralia, Mo., was shot to death in the streets of the former city, on the 29th, while being conveyed from the jail to the court house, where his trial was to take place. Corlew had been confined for some time past in the Kansas City jail as a precaution against lynching, an attempt having been made, soon after the villain's arrest, by a band of men from Centralia, to inflict summary punishment upon him. As stated above, Corlew was on his way to the court house, in charge of Sheriff Matlock, when the crowd opened fire upon him. At the first fire the doomed wretch was hit, but not hurt enough to disable him. He made a desperate effort for life and dashed into the court room, thinking perhaps that the sacred temple of justice would furnish a refuge. He was followed by three of the mob and shot again. With two bullets in his body, he escaped to the street and fell, but regained his feet and ran, receiving another shot. Still struggling to escape he ran through a dry goods store, into an alley and again into the street, with the slayers at his heels. He finally made his way up stairs over a saloon, and stood at bay, cornered like a rat. The husband of the woman he had outraged followed him and put five more bullets into his body, completing the bloody tragedy by putting his pistol to Corlew's forehead and sending a bullet through his brain. Notwithstanding all of his wounds Corlew lived ten minutes after the last shot was fired. During the horrible affair, the officers of the law seemed paralyzed with terror and made no effort to stop the butchery, although the killing was done so quickly that prevention would have been impossible.

A BLOODY FIGHT AT A CAMP MEETING.

A dispatch from Cincinnati, dated the 26th, says: The colored Baptist camp meeting at Danville, ten miles south of Hillsboro, O., was the scene, on Friday night and Sunday afternoon, of a bloody fight. On Friday night a party of drunken roughs went to the camp about 10 o'clock and began an attack with pistols, clubs and stones. They were repulsed and Wm. Diekman, one of their number, shot through the abdomen. Sunday afternoon, a party, said to number about 200, again attacked the camp, and a most desperate fight followed, ending in breaking up the meeting. It is thought some colored people were killed, but they dispersed so rapidly that the facts could not be gathered. No arrests were made.

A FOUL MURDER UNEARTHED.

Workingmen excavating near the relay depot at East St. Louis, came upon a long box which contained the decomposed remains of a man, whose right arm had been broken, whose throat had been cut, and on whose head there were several wounds. Over a year ago Judge Mayo, a banker at Olney, Ill., disappeared at this depot, and it has always been thought that he was enticed from a night train on some pretext, and murdered for his money. As the body discovered by the laborers is believed to be that of Judge Mayo, his friends have been notified.

A BURGLAR SHOT.

A dispatch from Council Bluffs, dated the 27th, says: At an early hour this morning one of two burglars was shot and killed while attempting to make an entrance into the residence of Hon. D. H. Salomon, on the latter's farm about thirty miles from this city, on the Wabash road. The fatal shot was fired by B. L. Salomon, son of D. H. The name of the dead burglar is not known.

ASSASSINATED.

A dispatch from Yazoo City, Miss., dated the 26th, says: Dr. M. F. Williams, of Mechanicsburg, was assassinated while riding home Saturday night. His horse reached home riderless and search being made the doctor's body was found. A negro was arrested on suspicion and has since confessed his guilt. He says he was paid to kill the doctor.

TWO OF THE NOTORIOUS BENDERS ARRESTED.

A dispatch from Fremont, Neb., dated the 29th, says: Two persons, a man and woman, past middle age, captured near here by Sheriff Gregg, are supposed to be old man Bender and Kate, the notorious murderers of Kansas. Both made a positive confession to-day. They will be held here until parties arrive from Kansas to identify them.

CHOKED HIS ASSAILANT TO DEATH,

John King stoned Paul Smith, a negro, in Correville, a Cincinnati suburb, until the fun became monotonous to the African, who turned and ran. King pursued, pelting the colored man with rocks. Finding that there was no escape, Smith seized his persecutor by the throat and literally choked him to death.

A CATTLE HERDER MURDERED.

A dispatch from Caldwell, Kan., dated

the 26th, says: A horrible murder was committed to-day. At 9 a.m. Chas. Wilson murdered W. H. Stephens, foreman of Maj. Hood's cattle men, thirty miles south of here. The body of the murdered man has just arrived, and the murderer will be here this evening.

THE WINTHROP TRAIN ROBBERS.

A dispatch from St. Joseph, dated the 24, says: The case of Ballard and Brooks, Winthrop train robbers, came up in the circuit court to-day. They waived formal examination, and bail was fixel at $5,000 each. At 7 o'clock this evening bail had not been procured. The case will come up at the September term.

KILLED, A POLICEMAN.

A man named Charley Norton kulled a policeman in Kokomo, Col., near Leadville, on the 23rd, and, soon after being placed in jail, was taken out by a mob and lynched. He admitted just before the boys swung him off that he had murdered three other men, and that the punishment was just.

A YOUNG WIFE ELOPES.

Herman Pitchshe, 56 years old, lived at Sedalia, Mo., with his young wife. She finally eloped with a youthful admirer, taking $2,800, her husband's entire fortune. The old man followed the couple to Chicago, where he learned that they had gone to Europe.

A BANK ROBBED.

A dispatch from Hartford, Conn., dated the 27th, says: Three or four men entered Middleton's savings bank during the absence at dinner of some officials, and engaging the clerks in conversation, accomplices robbed the vault of $8,500.

A FIENDISH CRIME.

Abraham Martin, of Abbeville, S. C., knocked his wife down and then, standing on her as he would on a log, chopped her shoulders and sides into shreds. They had been married thirty-five years, and had fourteen children.

STABBED IN A QUABREL.

Harmon McCoy, living four miles from Acola, Ill., was stabbed and killed by Elisha McCabe, aided by Joel Engle, during a quarrel on the night of the 25th. McCabe escaped, but Engle was arrested.

A CROOKED LICENSE CLERK.

Henry Moorman, the license clerk at Cincinnati, is said to have overcharged for licenses, and pocketed the difference. He will be investigated.

A LOTTERY SWINDLER ABRESTED.

The police of Burlington, Iowa, have arrested a young fellow named D. N. Kratzer for conducting a lottery swindle in that city.

A SAFE ROBBED.

Burglars blew open C. S. Woodworth & Co.'s safe at Marshalltown, Iowa, on the 28th, and secured $4,000 worth of securities.

HANGED BY A MOB.

George Washington, a colored murderer, was recently hanged by a mob, in the backwoods of Tennessee.

ISAIAH CARR, in Kent county, R. I., jail, awaiting examination on a charge of killing his nephew, was found dead in his cell on the 28th.

A DISPATCH from Denison, Texas, dated the 28th, says: "To-day near Gobson station, I. T., a party of Creeks attacked two Cherokees, and killed one and wounded the other. Two Creeks were hanged by the Cherokees Monday night, hence the reprisal."

THOMAS DELANA was fatally stabbed by his paramour in a Chicago restaurant on the 27th.

JOSEPH ENEAS, alias Hoffman, an American resident in Aspinwall, Panama, and claiming to be a merchant, was arrested on charge of putting into circulation counterfeit greenback United States notes. GEORGE BELL and Cleary, old offenders, were arrested at New York on the 27th, on charge of passing five counterfeit chicks on the National Bank of Baltimore and the Merchants' Bank of the same city, and obtaining $10,000.

A colored camp meeting near Hillsboro, O., was broken up on the 25th, by a gang of roughs, who commenced operations by attempting to demolish the sutler's tent and ended by tiring into the crowd. Three persons were badly, probably fainly injured, while several others were considerably hurt.

Pat Kelly and Jack Brown, of Rochester, Pa., have been on bad terms for two years. They met on the 25th and resolved on finding out who was the best man. Brown was badly beaten, and acknowledged that he was. Enraged at his being whipped, and after the fight was all over, he pulled out his revolver, and, remarking that Kelly would never again whip anybody, fired three shots at him in quick succession. It is believed that Kelly will die of the wounds.

H. P. Comegys, stenographer of the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe railroad office at Topeka, Ks., suicided on the 25th.

A dispatch from Winnepeg says while Constable Powers was crossing Red river with Mike Carroll, an escaped prisoner, Carroll upset the boat and both were drowned.

Fred Welcom was arrested at Cheyenne on the 24th for murdering John F. Turner, son of Sheriff Turner, of Utah county, in Echo Canon, Utah, July 12. Welcom confesses and gives the name of an accomplice. The murder was for theft and was extremely brutal.

Abraham Martin attacked his wife with an axe at Abbeville, S. C., on the 24th instant, inflicting fatal wounds. He became enraged because his wife upbraided him for infidelity.

joshua-mack-columbus-1880-08-11.A2:
Intimidation in Indiana.
thought
CINCINNATI, August 12.—Demeratic threats of driving the negroes out of Indiana are being put into execution in at least three counties.

Early yesterday morning a band of masked Kuklux attacked the house of an inoffensive negro named Joshua Mack, one mile from Columbus, Ind., broke open the door and windows, and dragged him from his bed, declaring with vile oaths that they would hang him, and that they intended to "clean out all the niggers in the county before the election." They ransacked the house for arms, and found none, and finally agreed to let Mack go on condition that he would immediately leave. After they had gone some distance he followed them into the road where others were waiting, when all mounted their horses and rode away. Soon after they had gone some distance he followed them into the road where others of the party were waiting, when all mounted their horses and rode away. Soon after the house of Mr. Walker, who has a farm rented on which the negro lives, was stoned, the party yelling, cursing, and threatening about it for a considerable time. At Bluffton and Shelbyville similar attempts at intimidation have been made.

mobile-mobile-1880-08-02.A1: MEMPHIS has so far escaped yellow fever this summer, but almost as bad a calamity threatens that unfortunate city. Ed. Shaw, a copper-colored, insolent, incendiary negro, is a candidate for sheriff of the county in which Memphis is situate, and as a renegade white man is an independent candidate, the probabilities are favorable for the election of the Senegambian Shaw over the Democratic nominee, Phil. T. Athy, for many years the efficient chief of police of Memphis. The county of Shelby has a majority of blacks, and, the color line having been drawn by Shaw and his white colleages of the carpet-bag stripe, there is great danger to the material welfare of the city. Memphis is to be pitied.
mobile-mobile-1880-08-02.A2:
Democratic Victory at Memphis.
MEMPHIS, Aug. 5.—The election for county officers to-day resulted in a victory for the Democrats. The vote of the city was 8,500. P. R. Athey, Democrat, nominated for sheriff, received 5,600; Ed. Shaw (colored) Republican, 2,300, and John Powell, Greenbacker, 500. Full returns from the county are not received, but the above figures will not be materially changed. Judge L. B. Harrigan, candidate for criminal court judge, was on both the Democrat and Republican tickets. His majority will not be less than 8,000. Salutes are being fired in honor of the victory.
mobile-mobile-1880-08-02.A5:
Police News.
English Charlie and Mike Reagan had a little friendly fist fight yesterday. A pair or so of green gogles will be sported for a few days.

John Lane and his wife Sallie had a little ball of their own yesterday. They could not decide a disputed point satisfactorily, and Dr. Porter was called on to do it for them this morning. The stronger vessel was fined five dollars.

Nobody appeared this morning to prosecute Wyatt Gramlin, colored, charged with illegal voting, he was discharged. Alex Samford, same charge, was referred to Esq. Spellman.

James Bolton, colored, will serve forty days for being disorderly yesterday; Thomas Miner, twenty days for fighting; F. Vanishe paid three dollars for punching a fellow-citizen, and Ed. Young five dollars for general cussedness.

The "bloody first" was a little too warm to be healthy for awhile yesterday. A vote was challenged, a knock down followed and a general melee ensued. Captain O'Haver had his clothing spattered with blood, and was compelled to knock down and drag out two or three rowdies before he could get room enough to have a free swing. A relief was summoned from the station house and the trouble soon calmed, the only consequence being a few bloody noses and b'ack eyes.

Edward Stark, colored, started a row in the Eighth ward yesterday afternoon and was taken in tow by Officers McParkland and Daly. A short distance from the polls they met Tom Garvey, who took Daly's place and allowed him to go to the relief of his comrade Brennan, whom he found nearly smothered in a jam of negroes. While in the act of clubbing a male content, however, some one threw a heavy paving rock at him and knocked him senseless to the ground. By this time Brennan had risen to his feet and in a few moments both the brave fellows were shoulder to shoulder and laying things low. At this opportune moment, when the excitement was a its highest, a deputy sheriff fired his pistol in the air, and the blacks scattered. Both officers are all right today.

While walking along Bull Run yesterday, Captain Forrest, night station house keeper, and his son met a negro named Bob Garnet, who took exceptions to their assertions that Shaw was badly whipped, and without provocation called the old man a liar. The Forrest blood arose to fever heat, and the Forrest cane descended on Garnet's granium. Garnet is a powerful man however, and warding the blow struck the cane from Forest's hand, and snatching a pistol which the latter was attempting to draw, struck him over the head with it, knocking him in the gutter, quickly following up the attack by striking the younger Forest in the head with the but end of the weapon. He then cocked it and retreated backward and out of sight. He has since been arrested.
mobile-mobile-1880-08-02.A6:
One of the Victims.
A colored man, named Dick Lyles, who works in a coal yard, got mixed in the row at the First ward yesterday, and came out badly beaten over the head. He managed to stagger several squares, reaching a point on Johnson avenue, within a few steps of his house, then fell in the street insensible. After laying for some time he was recognized and conveyed to his residence. This morning Lyles was reported considerably improved.
mobile-mobile-1880-08-02.A7: O'Haver, with two policemen, used every endeavor to prevent trouble and gave the negroes fair warning that a riot would occur despite all efforts, unless they desisted. About three in the afternoon, or a little before, the crowd turned loose, lit into the obstreperous, bulldozing darkies and cleaned them out beautifully. No one was seriously injured. A few bloody noses and sore heads was all.

mobile-mobile-1880-08-02.A9:
Merry Memphis.
A DAY DEVOTED TO THE ELECTION AND NIGHT
TO REJOICING—AN UNUSUAL TURNOUT.
[Special to the Clincinnati Commercial.]

MEMPHIS, TENN., August 5.—The most exciting election for thirty years terminated here to-day in the triumph of peace and order by a large majority. The chief interest centred in the position of sheriff, to which Philip R. Athy is chosen by 1,800 votes over Edward Shaw (colored), and by a fair majority over both Shaw and Powell, the latter a National.

The total vote cast in the county is about 16,000, the Nationals getting some 1,200 and Shaw about 6,500.

L. B. Horrigan is reelected criminal judge by fully 8,000 majority over Harry Hill, National.

All places of business were closed throughout the day, and the mercantile interests, with almost the entire white population, were earnest for the successful ticket.

The priesthood and clergy generally went to the polls for the first time on record, and old men who had not voted for years were conveyed to voting-places in carriages and then led to the ballot-box.

Mrs. Merriwether, Miss Moon, and one or two other ladies, exercised the right of suffrage, and many others wanted to.

The colored leader Shaw is a shrewd but unscrupulous citizen, and his success would have been regarded as a public calamity. Many of his own race voted square against him.

Intense enthusiasm prevails to-night, and cannon are booming in honor of the occasion. The successful candidates are among the best and purest citizens we have, and all have held office, proving faithful to their trusts.

ABIJAH CATLIN, of Harwinton.
THEY HAVE THE COUNT.
We have the count "" exultingly exe
"We have the count!" exultingly exclaim southern Democrats, and having the count they look calmly upon the rage of those who suffer by it, and sneer at the "vain things" imagined by those who would have political missionary work done in the South.

That the confidence of the southern Democratic counters in themselves is not misplaced has been strikingly illustrated in two recent elections, that in Alabama and that in Shelby county, Tennessee. The Republican State committee of Alabama have shown, by direct and overwhelming evidence, that the election there was a disgrace to the whole system of popular government, and that the great Democratic majority reported is a shameless swindle. The committee are justified in declaring that the purpose of the Democratic party in Alabama is to ignore, disregard and nullify the late constitutional amendments by disfranchising the entire colored population of the State."

The same process that gave in Alabama a Democratic majority of 75,000 was used in Shelby county, Tennessee. The city of Memphis is in this county. In an address by the Republican county committee are to be found these facts:

The First ward of Memphis contains, by the census just taken, 1,086 male persons over twenty-one years of age—587 white, 499 colored. The election returns give 1,168 Democratic, 167 Republican and 73 Greenback voters; total 1,408 votes, or 322 more than the entire voting population.

The Second ward census shows 656 male persons of voting age; white 507, colored 149. The vote returned was 554 Democratic, 79 Republican, 47 Greenback; total 680. The poll book shows the names of 363 persons who are not on the census roll.

In the Third ward the census gives the aggregate voting strength at 940, including 817 white and 133 colored. The vote returned was: Democratic, 1,015; Republican, 53; Greenback, 37.

The Ninth ward has, by the census, 643 males above twenty-one years of age—331 white and 312 colored. The vote of the ward was: Democratic, 140; Republican, 209; Greenback, 93; total, 442. Now, the signif-
mates above twenty-one years of age—351 white and 312 colored. The vote of the ward was: Democratic, 140; Republican, 209; Greenback, 93; total, 442. Now, the significant fact is, that in the Ninth ward there was one Republican judge, while in the other three the polls were wholly controlled by Democrats.

A feeble attempt to explain the size of the Democratic vote is made by saying that many colored men voted the Democratic ticket. This can be admitted, and still the fact will remain that the Democratic vote returned exceeds the number of the whole voting population.

The elections in Alabama and in Shelby county are specimens of the practice of a party which is preaching the maintenance at any cost of the right to a free ballot, which of course includes an honest count. General Hancock, who declared in his letter of acceptance that "it is only by a full vote, a free ballot and a fair count that the people can rule in fact," has not yet said anything in condemnation of these frauds, nor has any of the men or newspapers which support him. If General Hancock is elected it will be by those who "have the count" and will use it as they have in Alabama and Shelby county. Let our readers ask themselves if they can conscientiously give them aid and comfort in their wicked and audacious assault upon the true foundations of popular government.

yazoo-city-yazoo-city-1880-07.A2:
The Yazoo Buildozers.
WASHINGTON, July 25.

F. P. Dixon, the brother of H. N. Dixon, who was murdered by the Democrats of Yazoo county, Mississippi, has just returned to Washington from a visit to his former home, to which he went a short time ago, against the wishes of his friends, for the purpose of seeing his brother's wife before she died. When he reached Yazoo City Mrs. Dixon was dead. Since her husband's murder she has not left her house except to attend church and to go to his grave. She died of a broken heart, and it can be truthfully said that James Barksdale killed her as well as her brave husband, whose sole offense was opposition to the Democratic party. After her bereavement, Mrs. Dixon was continually tormented by the fear that the murderers of her husband would also murder her and her children, and she rapidly grew prematurely old, so that at her death she seemed twenty years older than she really was. The scene at her death-bed is described as remarkably impressive and affecting.

Mr. Dixon remained in Yazoo for a few days, although his friends believed that his life was in peril, for after his brother's murder he was driven out of the State by the murderers, who warned him that death awaited him if he should dare to return. He is as fearless as his brother was, and on one or two occasions he said to men whom he knew, that he was a supporter of Garfield, and that he believed that Garfield would be elected. These men at once informed him that they would not tolerate such talk in Yazoo, and that it would be safer to indulge in such expressions of opinion in Washington, to which place they advised him to return at once. The Yazoo Herald noticed his arrival and also his political views, and informed him, editorially, that such opinions were not wanted there. Even one of the most conservative farmers on the river, about three miles above the city, Nathaniel Ingraham by name, gave him the same warning while Dixon was making a social call upon the family. "I like you personally," said he, "but we can't have men here who talk as you do, and say that they hope and believe that Garfield will be elected. We don't intend that any votes shall be cast for Garfield here, and if you feel as you talk you had better return to the North." Mr. Dixon says that half a dozen colored men can not get together in the street in Yazoo without interruption from white Democrats, who declare that they shall not discuss politics, and forbid them to mention the Republican National ticket. He adds that it was the general expression of the Democrats in Yazoo whom he met that no votes should be cast for Garfield there, and that no discussion involving any support of the Republican party should be allowed.

Yazoo county, Mississippi, is solid for Hancock, or at least the chivalry of that section intend that it shall be on election day. Mr. F. P. Dixon, brother of H. M. Dixon, who was murdered by the chivalry of that section two years ago, has returned to Washington from Yazoo, and says that the Democrats will not permit any meetings in the county in the interest of General Garfield. There cannot, he says, be a gathering of five colored men which is not immediately broken up by the Democrats. Under the circumstances it is not too much to presume that Yazoo will be solid for Hancock—[Chicago Tribune.
yazoo-city-yazoo-city-1880-07.A7: Mr. F. P. Dixon, brother of Col. Dixon, whose foul assassination by Jim Barksdale cries to heaven for vengeance, recently went to Yazoo to be present at the death bed of the heartbroken wife of his murdered kinsman. While there he was warned to forbear talking Republicanism in that section, as he would probably not find it healthy, and some of the "best citizens of Kemper county" informed him that they did not intend that any votes should be cast for Garfield. The scheme of obliterating "sectional asperities" seems to be forging ahead in Mississippi with all the momentum that can be imparted to it by the public acknowledgement of the services of such patriots as Barksdale, who was a delegate to Cincinnati, and voted for the nomination of Hancock.
yazoo-city-yazoo-city-1880-07.A8: Mrs. Dixon, widow of the man shot by Barksdale, at Yazoo, for presuming to run for the office of Sheriff against the regular Democratic nominee, died a few days ago of a broken heart, and was mercifully permitted a burial beside the mangled body of her husband. Barksdale was a delegate to Cincinnati, and was an integral part of the "solid South" that turned the tide for Hancock, because of his devotion to the cause so dear to the Barksdales and Gullys. We may well borrow the prophetic words of Jefferson when he said: "I tremble for my country when I remember that God is just."—Dubuque Times.

CARTER HARRISON ON INSANITY.
Mr. Carter Harrison has been making a partisan speech. In many respects the effort was of a piece with other speeches made in behalf of the Democratic party. There was just one statement in it, however, which is worthy of comment. Referring to the question of Rebel claims, Mr. Harrison is reported as saying that "There is not a same man in the country who believes that there is the slightest danger that the Democratic party will allow the payment of a single dollar of Rebel claims, or that any Northern Congressman will dare vote for them." It is not likely that Mr. Harrison will deny this statement in this part of the country; if he should go South to make campaign speeches, however, he would not repeat it, and he might be tempted to follow Ward Hampton's example and repudiate his own words. The utterance would not be popular in the South; if believed, it would cost the Democratic party a great many votes in that section of the country.

Judging from this expression of Mr. Harrison's, it is fortunate that he is not the Superintendent of an insane asylum, but only Mayor of Chicago. He would not be the best Superintendent an insane asylum ever had, though he is "the best Mayor Chicago over had." His judgment of insanity is extremely untrustworthy if he sets down every man as demented who believes or fears that Democratic control of the General Government may lead to the payment of Rebel claims. Men in full possession of their faculties and accustomed to make proper use of them have not been at a loss to discover evi-
tles and accustomed to make proper use of them have not been at a loss to discover evidences of a purpose to secure payment of Hebel claims when the Democratic party, ruled by the Southern politicians in caucus, shall come into power. For the benefit of Mr. Harrison, who does not seem to have used his faculties for obtaining information upon this subject, we reprint from the records of Chatham County, Georgia, a sample of claims that may be found by the thousand in Southern States and in Washington:

[Book 2, page 206.]

STATE OF GEORGIA, CHATHAM COUNTY—Before me personally came Isaac M. Marsh, a resident of Savannah, Ga., who, being duty sworn, deposed and saith he was in possession and the lawful owner of the following-painted shaves at the time they were emancipated and made free by the United States Government—to-wit:

1 woman, Sarah, age 18... 1
1 woman, Ellen, age 35, and four children from 8 to 12 age... 5
1 woman, Ann, age 40, and four children from 8 to 11 age... 5
1 man, Charles, age about 40... 1
1 woman, Ellen, his wife, age about 60... 1
1 woman, Isabella, age about 18... 1
1 woman, Ribuo, age about 50... 1
1 man, Jim, age about 60... 1

Total... 10

Sworn to and subscribed betoro me this July 20, 1874.

Levil B. Harr, Notary Public and ex-officio Justice of the Peace, Chatham County, Ga. Recorded July 20, 1874.

Similar proofs of losses in slaves and other property have been filed in all parts of the South by persons who believe that the time will come when the "Yanks" shall be compelled to reimburse them for the losses incident to the War and the abolition of slavery. The significance of these claims fully appears from the fact that the Constitution of Maryland, after declaring that no law shall be passed which shall make the State Government liable for emancipated slaves, expressly

provides that the General Assembly "may adopt such measures as they may deem expedient to obtain from the United States compensation for such slaves, and to receive and distribute the same equitably to the persons entitled." This provision was adopted after the Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution of the United States was ratified, so it must have been designed to meet some future contingency for the repeal or nullification of that amendment. Is it evidence of insanity to take cognizance of these facts?

Relative to the constitutional amendment prohibiting the payment of the Rebel debt or claims for emancipated slaves, Mr. Harrison may be informed that one of the Democratic schemes, already fully foreshadowed, is the enlargement of the Supreme Court to the extent that may be necessary to give the Democrats control of that body. When that end shall have been accomplished, the payment of Rebel claims may be brought about without going through the form of repealing the Fourteenth Amendment. As to Northern Democratic Congressmen voting to pay Rebel claims, Mr. Harrison may as well conclude that Northern Democrats, as a rule, will vote as the caucus shall direct. His own vote against Shields is a case he perhaps can recall. The only incentive to the Democratic politicians of the North in this campaign is the possession of the offices, and the spoils will be denied to them by the caucus whenever they shall refuse to obey its instructions. From all this it may appear to Mr. Carter Harrison that he ought to revise his notions of insanity.

DEMOGRATIC METHODS IN THREE SOUTH-ERN STATES.

Reference to the political campaign as it is progressing in the States of Alabama, Mississippi, and Texas will show how the South proposes in November to establish "the principles for which Lee and Jackson fought," as Wade Hampton put it in his recent speech. Gen. Weaver, the Greenback candidate for President, who returned recently from his Fool's Errand in Alabama, has been talking with a representative of the Indianapolis Journal, and in the conversation expressed himself more freely than heretofore as to the Democratic methods in that State. During his visit there, the Bourbons made no secret of their determination that the Republicans should be counted out. As a proof of the manner in which it has been done, Gen. Weaver exhibited to the reporter a certified copy of the returns at the last four elections in Montgomery County, where the people are three-fourths Republican. At the Presidential election in 1876, Hayes' majority over Tildon was 3,881. At the Senatorial election in 1878, the Democratic majority was 1,060. At the Congressional election in 1878, Herbert, Democrat, was elected by 1,078 majority over Armstrong, Greenbacker. At the recent State election, Cobb, Democrat, was elected Governor over Pickens, Greenbacker, by 2,616 majority. Gen. Weaver also detailed some of the methods by which colored men are prevented from voting. Whenever one of them attempts to vote the Republican ticket he is challenged, and from fifteen to twenty minutes are occupied in questioning him, the result being that, by the time the polls are closed, there is a large crowd of negroes who are unable to vote. Another favorit method is to provoke a quarrel with a negro at the polls, and then send for a militia company and drive all the negroes away upon the pretense that they are violating the peace. The timid are kept away by notification that there will be trouble at the polls, and that their lives will be in danger. When all other methods to prevent them from voting fall, then they resort to the process of counting out, which is done by simply removing the Republican votes from the box and filling it up with Democratic votes, without regard to number, which accounts for the fact that in several counties at the recent election the returns show a larger Democratic vote than the total number of males over 21 years of age of all parties combined!

The Democratic methods are brought to their highest perfection in Mississippi, where no Republican can be elected, though the State has a clear Republican majority of 30,000. A correspondent of the St. Louis Globe-Democrat, who has been over the ground thoroughly, describes some of the methods in a letter to that paper.
yazoo-city-yazoo-city-1880-07.A11:
YAZOO, Aug. 24, 1880.
Dell, Forthead, Or.
I have just received a letter from Governor J. M. Stone, of this State, enclosing your letter to him of the 15th inst., with the accompanying article from the Daily Oregonian, containing an interview with Frank P. Dixon, published in the Chicago Times. The Governor informs me that he has written to you of the disposition of your letter, and of his request to me to give you the facts of the matter. It gives me pleasure to serve both you and him.

There is no truth in the article, or in the alleged statements made by Frank Dixon. He was never driven away from here. Up to the time of Henry Dixon's death he lived upon his brother's hounty, having no means of support of his own, having always lived the life of an idler. He came from near Washington City originally, and I presume his pecuniary necessities drove him back there. He was an utterly insignificant, timid and obscure young man, whom no one thought of harming, and was as safe as I am. He cut no figure whatever in politics.

Mrs. H. M. Dixon was greatly respected here, and always received the sympathy of the whole community in her distress. She was a native of the place, and had many very sincere friends here. The statement that she either feared molestation, or was in danger of it, is absurd.

There were no threats whatever made against Frank Dixon on his recent visit to the place. He was dally on the streets, and visited about the county at his pleasure. Mr. Nat. Ingram, whose name is mentioned in the interview, lived some distance up the river, on the opposite bank, and it would cause me some delay and trouble to communicate with him; but I assure you that he has publicly refuted so much of the statements as refers to him.
with him, but I assure you that he has publicly refuted so much of the statements as refers to him.

What is said about the action of the Yazoo Herald is as false as all the rest. I send you by same post with this, a copy of that paper marked, from which you will see exactly what it did say about Mr. Dixon. For fear it should not reach you, I copy the notice referred to in full. Here it is:

"Frank Dixon, now a resident of Washington City, has been on a visit to Yazoo for a few days."

That was everything—absolutely everything—it said about him. As you will see, it afterwards answered his slanders.

The greatest falshood of all, is the statement in the last paragraph, that a half dozen colored men cannot get together on the streets of Yazoo City without interruption from white democrats. Our streets are crowded with hundreds of them daily. They compose part of our fire department; have a fine hall; four large churches, some of them very handsome, where they congregate nightly and on every Sabbath. They
yazoo-city-yazoo-city-1880-07.A12:
are constantly seen in large processions,
and in excursions in great multitudes.
Yazoo county supports over one hundred public schools, more than two-thirds of which are for colored children.
Her treasury is full of money, and her teachers are paid promptly in cash.
The colored people have a fine state normal school, and a college of their own, supported by the public. The census of 1870 gave Yazoo county 17,000 inhabitants, and now in 1880, it gives her 35,000; and her people are rich, prosperous and happy. Many of the wealthy men are colored, and they own some of the finest and most valuable plantations in the county, as well as valuable real estate in this city. Immigrations, white and colored, are constantly coming in; and all who are industrious prosper.

These, I think, are the most effectual answers that can be given to the cruel falshoods told about us. No such prosperity could exist in the hell which the republican papers paint.

There is a full republican electoral ticket in the field, and any white man or darkey, who desires to do so, may vote for Garfield as freely as you may in Oregon.

Pardon the length of my letter. I could hardly answer in fewer words.

Yours truly,

GARRETT ANDREWS.
Yazoo City, Aug. 25, 1880.

yazoo-city-yazoo-city-1880-07.A13:
NORTHERN SLANDERS OF THE SOUTH.
A COMPLETE REFUTATION.
To the Editor of the Oregonian:
PORTLAND, Sept. 7, 1880.
I hand you herewith a letter from
I hand you herewith a letter from Gov. Stone, of Mississippi, and one from Garrett Andrews, Esq., of Yazoo City, enclosing an article published in your paper, from the Chicago Times, on the 15th of August last, together with responsible certificates of its falsehood in every line and letter. Acquainted as I am with the sentiments that animate Southern people, I knew the statements of F. P. Dixon to be false, though I was aware that thousands of well meaning people in the North believed every word, and more. These and like cruel and heartless calumnies filled me with a sense of injury and resentful wrong, and I enclosed the article to Gov. Stone, asking that he furnishme with a statement of the truth. He has done so. These resentless slanders are crimes against the public life, and being exposed in all their glaring enormity, should stir the indignation of an honest and generous people. If such crimes are fostered we shall become a nation of liars.

SIDNEY DELL.

JACKSON, Miss., Aug. 24, 1880.

Sidney Dell, Esq., Portland, Or.:

Your letter of the 10th inst., inclosing a letter from Washington to the Chicago Times, clipped from the Oregonian of the 10th inst., in relation to F. P. Dixon and his visit to Yazoo county, in this State, has been received. I regret that I am not sufficiently acquainted with the circumstances to which the correspondent refers to enable me to furnish such statement of facts as the courtesy of your inquiry demands, but I have referred the matter to Col. Garrett Andrews, a prominent citizen of Yazoo City, a gentleman who is conservative in all things, enjoys the confidence of all parties, and whose statements are entitled to the fullest credit. If Col. Andrews shall think proper to write you on the subject, I assure you that you may rely upon what he says with perfect confidence in its truth.

I know that Henry M. Dixon was killed by James A. Barksdale on account of a gross personal affront, and not by "the Democrats of Yazoo county," as stated. I do know that Mrs. Dixon died some time since, and I learned that she received the kindest attention and treatment from the people of Yazoo City during her illness, and her funeral was attended by a very large concourse of the best people of the town. Of course I cannot say what Mrs. Dixon's apprehensions were after the death of her husband, but I do say that if she had any feats for she and her children thee were utterly groundless.

I do not know what Mr. Ingraham or any one else said to Mr. F. P. Dixon, but the whole statement is so utterly at variance with the character and conduct of the people of Yazoo county, and so absurd in its details, that I do not hesitate to express the belief that it is a fabrication from beginning to end. Respectfully,

J. M. STONE.
